question: Retain rational square matrices A indexed by Fin n and a column support function c:Fin n→Fin n, with amp(j)=A(c(j),j) and reconstruction R_c(A)(i,j)=amp(j) if i=c(j), else0. The inherited convention describes support at the FIXED row c(j). State and prove the exact support condition for R_c(A)=A. Then distinguish two claims: (a) for every matrix with at most one nonzero per column there EXISTS a suitable c giving reconstruction; (b) any previously fixed c reconstructs every such matrix. Assess the historical demand to refute claim(a) with a column containing TWO nonzeros: is that a valid counterexample under its premise? Prove or refute each claim in the stated finite square setting, including n0. Give a genuine one-sparse counterexample to claim(b) for a specified c, a separate two-nonzero limitation example, and a correctly reconstructed target with a zero column. State why arithmetic reconstruction alone is not a normalizer-one block-encoding or oracle/circuit certificate.
reference_answer:
Write hSupport:forall i,j,i≠c(j) implies A(i,j)=0. At i=c(j), R_c(A)(i,j)=A(c(j),j)=A(i,j); away from that row it is0, so hSupport proves equality. Conversely reconstruction equality forces every off-support entry to be0. Thus the support predicate is necessary and sufficient. The complete oneSparse_from_support proof supplies the forward implication by exactly this case split; oneSparseMatrix_entry_if supplies the formula.

For claim(a), if n>0 and a column has a nonzero entry, choose its unique nonzero row as c(j); uniqueness follows from at-most-one nonzero. If the column is zero, choose any row, say0. Then all off-support entries vanish and the reconstruction is exact. At n0 columns/rows are empty, c is the unique empty function and equality is vacuous. Thus the finite square existential reconstruction statement is TRUE. This is an existence/finite-choice fact, not an efficient method for finding a support oracle.

Claim(b) is false when c is fixed independently of A. Take n2,c(0)=0,c(1)=1 and A=[[0,0],[1,0]]. Each column has at most one nonzero, but A(1,0)=1 lies off c(0)=0. Both sampled amplitudes are0, so R_c(A)=0≠A. This is a genuine counterexample respecting the one-sparse premise; it violates the fixed-map hSupport condition.

The historical example D=[[1,0],[1,0]] has two nonzeros in column0. Whichever c(0) is chosen, one nonzero is off-support, so no map reconstructs D. But D violates the premise of claim(a), hence cannot refute it. It only demonstrates the limitation on non-one-sparse inputs. Finally B=[[0,0],[0,3]], with c0=0,c1=1, has amp0=0,amp1=3 and reconstructs exactly: the entire zero column is allowed. These examples retain rational entries; zero amplitudes need no choice of a distinguished nonzero row.

The reconstructed B has operator norm3, so this arithmetic equality is not a normalizer-one unitary compression. Normalization, unitary completion, reversible location-map implementation, amplitude loading, ancilla cleanup, finite-bit evaluation and resource costs are separate obligations; a support map function need not itself be injective or an already supplied reversible oracle. The empty case does not require selecting a row from an empty carrier because there are also no columns. No invalid two-nonzero refutation or quantum synthesis conclusion is retained.

exposition.core_summary: The fixed-c reconstruction is equivalent to off-support zero entries; suitable c exists for every finite square one-sparse matrix, while a mismatched fixed c can fail and a two-nonzero column is not a counterexample to the existential premise. Zero columns and correctly located single nonzeros reconstruct exactly, including the empty square case; this entrywise identity does not supply unitary normalization or oracle/circuit resources.
